views.reconstructed_statement: For every natural number k and every pair of real-coefficient polynomials p,q, if natDegree(p) <= 2*k+1 and natDegree(q) <= 2*k+1, and for every natural j with 0 <= j <= k their j-fold ordinary polynomial derivatives agree at -1, and for every such j their derivatives agree at 0, then p=q as polynomials. The j=0 conditions are agreement of polynomial values. The statement is uniqueness within the indicated degree bound for two prescribed endpoint jets; it does not itself assert existence for arbitrary data, an exact degree for p or q, or degree minimality.

ambient_definitions.coprimality: IsCoprime(A_k,B_k) is polynomial coprimality, expressible by a Bezout combination equal to 1.
ambient_definitions.divisibility: f divides g means polynomial divisibility in R[X], hence existence of a polynomial h with g=f*h.

derivative_and_degree_conventions: derivative^[j] is j-fold iteration of the ordinary algebraic polynomial derivative; derivative^[0] p=p. It is not a Hasse derivative or a Taylor coefficient.
Taylor(a,p)=p(X+a), so coefficient j of Taylor(a,p) is p^(j)(a)/j! over R. The supplied interface states p^(j)(a)=j!*coeff_j(Taylor(a,p)); the factorial is cast to R.
natDegree takes values in N and natDegree(0)=0. The root bounds natDegree, including the zero case; it does not use a nonzero-polynomial hypothesis.

For a nonzero polynomial, natDegree is its actual usual degree. A zero polynomial need not be assigned usual degree zero under a convention using degree(0)=-infinity; that separate convention does not change the supplied natDegree inequalities.
The upper bound is 2*k+1, not a statement that either input has exactly that degree or that this degree is minimal for any particular data.
domains_and_quantifiers: k ranges over all natural numbers, including zero.
p and q range independently over all elements of R[X], including the zero polynomial.
Each endpoint hypothesis quantifies j over N and assumes j<=k; these are the orders 0,1,...,k inclusive.
There is no analytic-function domain, interval assumption, positivity assumption on p or q, or approximation parameter.

For all k,p,q, the order-0-through-k jet equalities at 0 imply B_k divides p-q; endpoint specialization of n01. No degree hypothesis occurs.

Root uniqueness statement: apply the product-divisibility and low-degree vanishing interfaces to the difference p-q under the two input degree bounds.

views.reconstructed_statement: For every real a, every natural k, and every function v:N->R, let P=jetPolynomial(a,k,v)=sum_{j=0}^k (v(j)/j!)*(X-a)^j. Then natDegree(P)<=k, and for every natural j<=k, the j-fold ordinary derivative of P evaluated at a equals v(j). There are no restrictions on the values of v. Only its first k+1 values enter the polynomial. This is a degree-bound and interpolation statement for the displayed polynomial; the root does not assert that its degree is exactly k or formulate a least-degree optimization or uniqueness conclusion.

semantic_slots.conclusion_structure: A conjunction: the degree bound and the full ordinary-derivative matching assertion through order k.

construction.data_used: Only v(0),...,v(k) occur in the finite sum; values v(j) for j>k do not affect P.
construction.factorial_convention: j! is cast from N to R before division; it is nonzero for every j, including 0!=1.
construction.literal_definition: def jetPolynomial (a : ℝ) (k : ℕ) (v : ℕ → ℝ) : ℝ[X] := taylor (-a) (∑ j ∈ Finset.range (k + 1), monomial j (v j / (j.factorial : ℝ)))
construction.shift_convention: Taylor(b,Q)=Q(X+b). Thus Taylor(-a, sum_j monomial(j,v(j)/j!)) shifts the origin polynomial to powers (X-a)^j; Taylor(a,P) shifts back.

derivative_and_degree_conventions: derivative^[j] is the ordinary algebraic j-fold derivative, not divided derivatives. P^(0)(a)=P(a)=v(0). The coefficients in powers (X-a)^j are v(j)/j!, not v(j).
The conclusion is natDegree(P)<=k. natDegree(0)=0, so the all-zero prescribed prefix is included.

For nonzero P its actual degree can be lower than k. From the displayed formula, if some v(j) with j<=k is nonzero, the degree is the largest such index; in particular degree k requires v(k) nonzero. This is an interpretation of the formula, not an extra claim in the root.
If v(0),...,v(k) all vanish, P=0, natDegree(P)=0, and usual degree may instead use a separate zero-polynomial convention such as -infinity.
The root supplies neither a quantified comparison against other candidate polynomials nor an explicit minimality or uniqueness assertion. It also makes no equality assertion with v(j) for j>k.

k ranges over all N, including zero.
v ranges over all functions N->R, without finite-support, regularity, nonzero, or compatibility assumptions.
j in the derivative conclusion ranges over all N subject to j<=k.
